THOUGHT: This 40-year-old woman presents with a 5-month history of chronic bladder discomfort relieved by voiding, urinary frequency (10–15/day), nocturia (2–3/night), and dyspareunia — all in the absence of objective signs of infection (negative urinalysis for WBCs, nitrites, leukocyte esterase, bacteria; no fever or systemic symptoms) and with normal imaging (pelvic ultrasound showing minimal postvoid residual) and cystoscopy (no mucosal lesions, Hunner’s ulcers, or masses). Her suprapubic tenderness on abdominal and bimanual exam, along with pain exacerbated by bladder filling and relieved by voiding, is highly characteristic of bladder-centered chronic pelvic pain. Importantly, she is on lithium — a known risk factor for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI), which can cause polyuria and secondary bladder irritation; however, her urine specific gravity is normal (1.010), and she does not report polydipsia or large-volume voiding — making NDI unlikely. The absence of hematuria, infection, obstruction, stones, malignancy, or structural abnormality rules out common urologic mimics. Her symptom constellation — chronic pelvic pain localized to the bladder, urinary frequency without incontinence, pain relief with voiding, and dyspareunia — aligns precisely with the clinical criteria for interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS), as defined by the American Urological Association (AUA) and EAU. IC/BPS is a diagnosis of exclusion but supported strongly here by: (1) chronic (>6 weeks) bladder discomfort/frequency, (2) symptom relief with voiding, (3) absence of infection or other identifiable cause, (4) negative cystoscopy (though hydrodistension was not performed — not required for diagnosis), and (5) reproducible suprapubic/bladder tenderness on exam. Dyspareunia is a common associated symptom due to pelvic floor myalgia and central sensitization often comorbid with IC/BPS.

DIAGNOSIS: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome
